title: 7 Roles as a Christian Employer
paragraphs: 7 Roles as a Christian Employer
He signs the paycheck… but Heaven is watching how he treats the people behind it.
That’s the tension.

Because being a Christian employer isn’t just about profit.
It’s about pastoral responsibility in the marketplace.
And many miss this.

They pray loud on Sunday…
but lead harshly on Monday.

But here’s what we miss…
God never separates your leadership from your discipleship.
If Christ is Lord—He’s Lord of your company too.
So what does that look like?
🔥 7 Roles of a Christian Employer

1. Steward, not owner
This business? It’s not yours.
It’s entrusted to you.

“Whatever you do… do it all for the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)
You manage what belongs to Him.

2. Shepherd, not just boss
People under you are not tools.
They are souls.

You don’t just assign tasks—
you care, correct, and cover them in prayer.

3. Justice-bringer
No favoritism. No exploitation. No hidden oppression.

“Masters, treat your workers justly and fairly…” (Colossians 4:1)
God watches how you handle power.

4. Provider with integrity
Pay right. Speak truth. Cut no corners.
A Christian employer doesn’t build success on hidden sin.

5. Culture-setter
Your workplace has a spirit.

You decide if it’s toxic…
or if it breathes honor, excellence, and peace.

6. Discipler through example
They may never read the Bible—
but they will read you.

Your patience. Your humility. Your repentance.
That’s daily preaching.

7. Servant leader
This is where it flips.
Jesus said, “Whoever wants to be great must be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26)

You don’t climb over people.
You lift them.
And here’s the Gospel truth…
You won’t lead perfectly.

You’ll fail.
Lose your temper.
Make selfish calls.
But Jesus didn’t die only for your Sunday sins.
He died for your leadership sins too.

On the cross, Christ paid for every moment you led out of pride instead of love.
And in His resurrection, He gives you power to lead differently.
Not perfectly. But faithfully.

So repent where needed.
Realign your leadership.
And let your workplace become a place where grace is seen—not just spoken.
Because this matters.
